title: Maduro pleads not guilty to new torture-related charges in New York
content: Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, appeared in court on Thursday to plead not guilty to new charges of conspiracy to commit torture. The US government initially accused Maduro of narco-terrorism, drug trafficking and weapons-related offenses, before adding new charges against him and Flores last week. Maduro and Flores were captured in January during a US military raid, after which they were taken to New York, where they remain in jail. The couple has pleaded not guilty to the allegations and both have argued to have the case thrown out on the grounds that they qualify for sovereign immunity. Their trial is scheduled for June 2027. In a new indictment last week, government prosecutors alleged Maduro and Flores "created and maintained a violent system of repression" that saw "thousands of Venezuelans" killed, harassed, and tortured. Nicolas Maduro denied the new charges brought against him by the US government, telling a court on Thursday he denied the "false accusations and false testimony behind him." "I reject this document entirely," Maduro said in Spanish through a translator. Judge Alvin Hellerstein interrupted Maduro, and declared the court would enter a plea of not guilty for Maduro. "I am completely innocent. I am not guilty," Flores said through a translator. Maduro and Flores wore beige jail uniforms and both appear to have lost weight during their detention in Brooklyn. The alleged torture methods included "electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture", the indictment states. The US also accused Maduro of authorising the use of torture "against specific individuals" and alleges US citizens were tortured under this system. Prosecutors already have accused Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices of engaging in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnering with cartels designated as terrorist groups. Maduro previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves. He and his wife's lawyers have argued that Maduro is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal. Flores unsuccessfully petitioned a judge to allow her to be released on bond while she awaited trial, arguing she had heart problems and other health issues while detained at the notorious Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn. Anna Fraine describes the extent of the damage caused by two earthquakes in June as "just immense". The planned firing-squad execution on 3 December has led to questions about legality and purpose. Pete Hegseth says the execution will be public, but a legal expert says the "unprecedented" decision is on "uncertain legal terrain". Bassam al-Hassan is being sheltered in return for information - including about abducted US reporter Austin Tice. River's ex-housemate, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, testified he had no idea about his activities. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
content: US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad. Trump had previously said he approved of showing the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it. Trump's decision to cancel the livestream came after widespread criticism in the US and globally. On Thursday, he said that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die". "I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump said. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," the president added. Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US military personnel and injured 32 others at a military base in Texas in 2009. His execution by firing squad will be the first military execution in more than 60 years. Trump said the families of the victims can still view the execution in person if they wish. "They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" he said. After the Pentagon announced last week that it would execute Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad and livestream the event, a cascade of criticism quickly followed from human rights groups and many others. The United Nations called the plans "abhorrent". While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. According to Amnesty International, 11 public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth defended his decision to air Hasan's execution online, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things". But as criticism mounted, Trump appeared to hedge his support, saying on Friday that he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but adding that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it. The president also called Hasan "totally nuts". "I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him," he said. After Trump announced he called it off, a Pentagon spokesman said Hegseth had spoken with the US president beforehand. "The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," the spokesman Sean Parnell said. John Galligan, a lawyer for Hasan working primarily on civil issues, told the BBC that Trump's decision to cancel the livestream of his execution "comes as no surprise". "It was initially a dumb decision and statement by Hegseth to livestream any execution - and it violated the Army's own regulation," Galligan said. He said Hasan is paralysed from the chest down, something that Trump "allegedly didn't even know" when he approved the livestream plan. "The damage has already been done - the Army is now just trying to clean up the mess," Galligan said. "It will permanently remain a stain on our military justice system." He added that it was not clear if Hasan was aware yet of Trump's "reversal" of the livestream decision. Hasan opened fire in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines. He later admitted in court that he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base. US military law requires that a military execution be approved by the US president. It also requires appellate review, when a higher court inspects the decision and gives a final judgement on its legality to move forward. Livestreaming the execution of Nidal Hasan "will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it," 72 former officers said in a letter. A series of calls, obtained by the Associated Press, reveal emergency services were delayed in reaching Pike. Markwayne Mullin rejects concerns that livestreaming the execution of convicted killer Nidal Hasan could fuel radicalisation or make him a martyr. The planned firing-squad execution on 3 December has led to questions about legality and purpose. The planned execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad would be the first military execution in more than 60 years. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: US teenager appears in court over alleged Hindu temple shooting plot
content: A man has been arrested after an investigation into threats of a potential mass shooting that could have targeted a Hindu temple near Chicago. Alexandros Paporakis, 19, from Palatine, Illinois, appeared in court on Wednesday. He was charged with one count of making a terrorist threat and one count of unlawful possession of a weapon for possessing a rifle with a barrel less than 16in long, the BBC's US partner CBS reports. Police said they found a manifesto in which Paporakis identified as a white supremacist and wrote about his hatred for non-white people. Prosecutors said the defendant told a colleague on the phone that his gun jammed and sent messages showing an AR-style rifle, CBS reports. Other messages showed how the gun failed to fire when he pulled the trigger, and a photo of himself in a tactical vest, according to prosecutors. This colleague and another coworker from the Taco Bell where Paporakis worked called police on Sunday to report the incident. Palatine Police Chief William Nord said that officers "recovered a rifle, they recovered loaded magazines, hundreds of rounds of rifle ammunition, as well as body armour," while searching Paporakis' home. Officers and the FBI were also able to examine Paporakis' electronics and electronic communications, where they said they found the manifesto. "Reading through the manifesto, he did state some extremist ideologies and talked about violence, he talked about mass killings and how he wanted to carry out this mass shooting," Nord said, according to CBS. Prosecutors allege that Paporakis' colleague told police the defendant had spoken about being a white supremacist while at work, and made disparaging comments about people of other races. Prosecutors said that on Saturday, Paporakis told a worker he was planning "it" at a Hindu temple in Aurora, and said Sunday "was going to be a special day", before calling and sending the messages to his colleague the next day. Police said that a specific intended location in the alleged threats has not been confirmed, and the investigation remains open. Local Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi said he was "horrified" by the incident. In a statement posted on Facebook, he said: "Every American deserves to live and worship without fear, and we must stand together against hatred in all its forms." Trump said some would "rather not watch" the killing of Nidal Hasan, the first military execution in over 60 years. The nature of the investigation is unclear but comes after officials cast doubt on her US citizenship. Katie Zacharia does not appear to be registered to the legal bar in any state where she has lived. The Since U Been Gone singer claims she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" an item in the store. Democrats and Republicans alike are coming out against data centre development, amid growing backlash across the US. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved.
